title: The Math of the Lottery
objective: After this level you can compare the odds of winning a big jackpot with everyday chances and explain why a ticket's expected value is below its price.
summary: A $2 Powerball play has a 1 in 292,201,338 jackpot chance, far less than a lightning strike in a year. About half of sales go to prizes, so a play returns about $1 on average.

cards.headline: A $2 Powerball play has a 1 in 292,201,338 chance at the jackpot.
cards.body: A number that big barely means anything. Let's make it mean something, then ask what the ticket is really worth.

cards.headline: One ticket a second, for 9 years
cards.body: To hit the jackpot you must match 5 numbers from 1 to 69 plus a Powerball from 1 to 26. Say you bought one ticket every second, day and night, never repeating. A day has 86,400 seconds, so covering all 292 million combinations would take more than 9 years. At the end, you'd hold exactly one jackpot winner.

mascot.line: This is Level 8's trick again: turn a huge count into seconds, and you can feel how big it is.

cards.headline: Lightning is the likelier story
cards.body: Based on 2009 to 2018 averages, the National Weather Service puts your odds of being struck by lightning in a given year at 1 in 1,222,000. Divide the jackpot odds by that and you get about 239. So in any year, a lightning strike is more than 200 times as likely as one ticket winning the jackpot.

cards.fact: About half of every dollar played goes back out as prizes.
cards.context: So across all tickets sold, a $2 play returns about $1 in prizes on average: its expected value is well below its price. About 1 in 25 plays does win something (the official odds are 1 in 24.87), but the smallest prizes are $4 and $7.

cards.headline: The lottery: priced
learned: One ticket a second for over 9 years
A lightning strike is over 200 times likelier
A $2 play returns about $1 on average

questions.prompt: What are the odds of winning the Powerball jackpot with one play?

options.label: About 1 in 25
options.rationale: That's the chance of winning any prize, usually a small one.

options.label: About 1 in 1.2 million
options.rationale: That's the yearly chance of a lightning strike.

options.label: About 1 in 29 million
options.rationale: Ten times too likely; the jackpot is 1 in 292,201,338.

questions.explanation: The jackpot odds are 1 in 292,201,338 per $2 play.

questions.prompt: How can you tell a $2 Powerball play has an expected value below its price?

options.label: Most players never win anything
options.rationale: True for most plays, but the expected value comes from how much goes to prizes.

options.label: About half of each dollar played goes to prizes
The jackpot odds are too long to count
options.rationale: Long odds alone do not set the expected value; the prize money does.

options.label: The smallest prize is only $4
options.rationale: Small prizes are part of it, but the key is that prizes total about half of sales.

questions.explanation: Prizes total about 50% of sales, so on average a $2 play returns about $1.

questions.prompt: Level 8 said a day has 86,400 seconds. Buying one Powerball combination per second, how long to buy all of them?

options.label: About 3 days
options.rationale: That's about 292,000 seconds, a thousand times too few.

options.label: About 9 months
options.rationale: Still far too short for 292 million seconds.

questions.explanation: 292,201,338 ÷ 86,400 is about 3,382 days, a little over 9 years.
